title: DeepSeek ships V4.1 Flash into production, plans to route V4 Pro traffic to it
subtitle: A two-day beta under the temporary model ID `deepseek-v4.1-flash-expires-on-0910` closes today, replaced by a native-multimodal production model that will absorb V4 Pro API traffic by September 14.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: DeepSeek opened a two-day API beta for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on September 8, 2026, under a temporary model identifier — `deepseek-v4.1-flash-expires-on-0910` — with a hard 20-concurrent-request cap per account. That endpoint shut down today, September 10, and DeepSeek shipped the production model string `deepseek-v4.1-flash` in its place. After 12:00 Beijing Time on September 14, all requests to `deepseek-v4-pro` will be routed to V4.1 Flash and billed at the V4.1 Flash price. DeepSeek describes the architecture as a new native-multimodal design — text, image, and audio through a single stack — with community and press-relayed throughput tests reporting sustained 300–355 tokens per second and peaks above 500 tok/s.

Two things are notable in how this shipped. First, the temporary model ID with an explicit expiration date encoded in the name is DeepSeek's second use of that convention this year — an unusually blunt way to keep beta and production traffic from co-mingling, and one that makes the eventual routing easier to reason about. Second, DeepSeek is doing what has been rare in the frontier this year: cannibalizing its own paid tier. Rather than letting V4 Pro coexist as a premium option, DeepSeek is redirecting all Pro traffic to Flash at the Flash price. That is either a confidence signal that V4.1 Flash matches V4 Pro on the workloads customers actually use — or a margin decision that Flash's inference cost is now low enough to serve every request through it.

The launch also lands in an awkward political week. The CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA26-251A published September 8 names DeepSeek first among six Chinese firms accused of industrial-scale distillation from US frontier models. Whether V4.1 Flash's capability jump is downstream of that campaign is exactly the question US providers will now be under quiet federal pressure to consider before serving DeepSeek-adjacent API traffic. For DeepSeek, the response so far has been to ship faster and cheaper: the 300+ tok/s throughput and the Flash-price migration are the announcement, and the advisory is not in the changelog.

Takeaway for learners: pay attention to how a lab names its beta endpoints — the operational vocabulary they use tells you what they optimize for. DeepSeek's `expires-on-0910` string is a design choice about trust and cleanup: no lingering beta, no free grandfathered tier, no ambiguity about which model your production traffic hits after the migration date. When you build API surfaces of your own, that pattern — an explicit sunset baked into the identifier — is a durable one worth stealing.
